newsitem.title: DENMARK: Danish police fear reprisals after biker attack. [CORRECTED 20:15 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Danish police fear reprisals after biker attack. [CORRECTED 20:15 GMT]

text.p: Danish police were on the alert for revenge attacks on Sunday, after a missile strike on a Hell's Angels biker gang party killed two people and wounded 19, in the bloodiest incident yet of a Nordic biker war.
Police named the victims as 38-year-old Louis Nielsen, a candidate for Hell's Angels membership and Janne Krohn, 29, a woman party guest with no known connection to the bike gangs.
"We are always concerned about the possibility of a Hell's Angels revenge attack," city deputy police chief Henning Thiesen told a news conference.
"We, of course, are trying to predict where possible reprisal actions may occur but it is not us who chooses the time, place or weapon," he said.

Police said that of 11 people still in hospital after the missile ploughed through the walls of a Hell's Angels' clubhouse in Copenhagen's Noerrebro, two were seriously injured, one of them in a life-threatening condition.
Another eight people were discharged after treatment.

Prime suspects were the Bandidos bike gang, like the Hell's Angels offshoots of a U.S. group. The two have been battling for supremacy in Denmark, Finland, Norway and Sweden almost since the Bandidos set up shop in the region in the summer of 1993.

Immediately after the 0105 GMT rocket attack police raided several known Bandido properties around the country, but by mid-afternoon had made only two arrests, neither connected with the missile blast, they said.
Police were checking passengers leaving by ferry for nearby Sweden and monitoring travellers leaving by air, they added.

The missile was fired into the back of the clubhouse from a nearby rooftop and the attacker escaped, evading a police cordon designed to pre-empt any raid on the Hell's Angels' annual "Viking Party", held despite a previous bomb attempt.

Denying any laxity by police, Thiesen said that the Angels themselves must take part of the responsibility for the attack by going ahead with a high-profile party for some 300 people at a time when the building was a known target for a Bandido raid.

"We cannot guarantee full security if people want to kill in this way, I am tempted to say "if people want to be killed', because it was absolutely reprehensible to hold a party under the present conditions and gather so many people," he said.

But a source close to one of the gangs said that for the Hell's Angels -- biggest and most senior of the major international bike gangs -- to cancel the party for fear of attack would have brought unthinkable loss of face.
The same code compels the Angels to take revenge for the humiliating attack on the heavily-fortified Noerrobro house, bar and workshop complex, the gang's Danish flagship.
A Bandidos member was arrested in July after a bungled bomb attempt on the clubhouse, in which a six kg (13 pound) bag of exlosives was hurled from a car but failed to explode.

Shortly after Sunday's attack police found a spent launcher (corrects to make clear that the police made the discovery), and another with a live missile ready for firing, on the roof of a one-story building some 70 metres (yards) away.
They said that the weapons were among 12 stolen from a military weapons store in neighbouring Sweden in February 1994.
Missiles identified as from the stolen batch were fired at two Hell's Angels' clubhouses in Denmark last April.
Last March, attackers shot a Bandidos leader in the Finnish capital, Helsinki, and a Danish Bandido died in an ambush outside Copenhagen airport 10 days later.
A Danish Bandidos member was shot in the head near the Norwegian city of Drammen in July.
